criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking water and sewer service access in Ecuador across urban/rural areas, regions, and income quintiles.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: This paper passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it discusses Ecuador's 2008 Constitution (Art. 318), institutional fragmentation across SENAGUA, MIDUVI, MAE, and MSP, suspended water legislation, private concessions (e.g., INTERAGUA in Guayaquil), and public investment programs. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is no because the paper focuses on macro-governance background, inter-ministerial coordination overlap, and public investment program descriptions rather than empirically analysing a specific rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff rules, disconnection/enforcement, or regulatory rules) directly governing household service access. Under both readings, however, the full-text decision is exclude due to the absence of empirical methodology and study design (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical research method, primary data collection, secondary data analysis, or systematic empirical synthesis is present. The 5-page article is a narrative policy and human-rights overview that cites descriptive aggregate statistics from official reports (INEC censuses, SENPLADES MDG report, MIDUVI estimates) as country background before offering narrative commentary on institutions, draft laws, and investment programs. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive secondary statistics from national censuses and living condition surveys on residential piped water coverage, public sewer connections, and service continuity (permanent access).
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or empirical test linking a defined governance exposure to a service access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (translated into English as noted in the Acknowledgments).

evidence_quotes.quote: According to the National Institute of Statistics and Census’s (INEC) data, Ecuador’s percentage of residential access to piped water has progressively increased; 1990 census shows that 40.6% houses received this service.

Living conditions data from 2006 also reveal that access to piped water does not ensure permanent access to this service or to drinking water quality; at the national level, only 33% of homes with a piped water system received this service permanently.

Even after the constitutional changes in 2008, there have been no clear policies for integral environment sanitation. Although there is a growing public investment in drinking water systems and sanitation, there are also overlapping policies, objectives, functions, and responsibilities;

Besides SENAGUA, there are also other entities with jurisdiction over one or more aspects in water management: among others, MIDUVI, the Environment Ministry (MAE), the Public Health Ministry (MSP), the National Irrigation Institute (INAR), municipalities and provincial councils.

With regard to the new regulations, the approval of the Water Resources, Uses and Management Act has been suspended. This law should give more empowerment to the unique water authority so that it can be consolidated as the governing water entity.

raw_response.exposure: Macro-level constitutional, institutional, and public investment framework for water and sanitation in Ecuador (2008 Constitution, overlapping national ministries, pending legislation, and municipal concessions); not empirically analysed
raw_response.outcome: Descriptive national and regional rates of residential piped water access, public sewer network connection, and permanent service continuity cited from secondary official reports
raw_response.population_and_sample: Ecuadorian households cited descriptively from secondary official census and survey reports (1990 and 2001 INEC censuses, 2006 living conditions survey); no empirical study sample
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). This 5-page article is a narrative policy and institutional commentary on the right to water and sanitation in Ecuador following the 2008 Constitution. While it cites descriptive aggregate coverage statistics from national censuses and government reports as background, it contains no empirical methodology, primary data, original secondary analysis, systematic synthesis, or identifiable study design, and it discusses macro-level institutional overlap and investment programs rather than empirically evaluating a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing household access.
